lesson.title: Picnic pizza: the whole and its equal parts

blocks.text: At our fictional picnic, Alex brings one round pizza. The whole means the complete pizza before anyone takes slices. A fraction tells us about equal parts of that whole. Equal parts contain the same amount of pizza, even when they sit in different places.
blocks.title: Start with one whole pizza

blocks.text: Picture the same round pizza cut in two different ways. A straight cut through the centre makes two equal halves. A cut near the edge makes two unequal pieces. Each unequal piece is not one half of the pizza.

nodes.label: One whole pizza
nodes.detail: The complete round pizza is the whole we are sharing.

nodes.label: Cut through the centre
nodes.detail: The two pieces contain equal amounts, so each is one half.

nodes.label: Cut near the edge
nodes.detail: One piece is smaller, so these pieces are not halves.

blocks.title: Two pieces do not always mean two halves

blocks.text: Alex cuts the whole pizza into four equal slices. First, count all four equal slices in the whole. Next, Alex takes one slice and leaves three slices. We write Alex’s share as 1/4, meaning one quarter. The bottom number, called the denominator, counts all equal parts. The top number, called the numerator, counts the selected parts.

blocks.text: These strips stand for pizzas with the same total size. The shaded part shows the amount someone takes to eat. One half is more pizza than one quarter here. Two quarters contain the same amount as one half.

nodes.detail: One of two equal parts is shaded in this whole.

nodes.detail: Two of four equal parts cover half of this whole.

blocks.title: Compare shares from same-sized pizzas

lesson.purpose: Use a fictional picnic to identify one whole pizza, recognise equal parts, and compare simple fractions of same-sized pizzas in about ten minutes.

activity.prompt: Sam cuts one pizza into three pieces of equal size. Sam takes one piece, so which description is correct?
options: Sam takes 1/3 because the whole has three equal parts.
Sam takes 1/2 because two pieces remain on the plate.
Sam takes 3/1 because the pizza has three pieces.
activity.explanation: The whole has three equal parts, and Sam selects one. That makes Sam’s share one third, written as 1/3.

criteria.description: Identifies each complete pizza as a whole and identifies only Jo’s equal pieces as halves.
Writes Pat’s share as 1/4 and states that Jo’s half is more pizza.
Explains that halves must contain equal amounts and that 1/4 selects one of four equal parts.
States that the whole pizzas must be the same size for the half-versus-quarter amount comparison used here.

lesson.teachBackPrompt: Explain in your own words why two pieces are not always two halves. Use 1/4 to explain what the top and bottom numbers count, and say why pizza size matters when comparing shares.
lesson.applicationPrompt: At a new picnic, Jo and Lee have same-sized whole pizzas. Jo cuts one pizza through its centre into two equal pieces. Lee cuts the other near its edge, making one small piece and one large piece. In words, identify the whole for each person and explain whose pieces are halves. Then Jo takes one half, while Pat takes one of four equal slices from another same-sized pizza. Write Pat’s fraction and say who takes more pizza.

references.title: Visualize Fractions, OpenStax
references.summary: A fraction describes selected equal parts of a whole, with the denominator counting all equal parts and the numerator counting selected parts. Comparisons require attention to the whole being represented.

blocks.text:
At Alex’s fictional picnic, take the complete round pizza as the whole. A partition is a division of that whole into pieces. To describe individual pieces as halves or quarters, the partition must be equal: each piece must contain the same amount of pizza. Position does not determine equality; amount does. A cut through the centre produces two equal halves, whereas a cut near the edge produces a smaller and a larger piece, neither of which is one half.

In fraction notation, the denominator—the bottom number—counts all equal parts in the whole. The numerator—the top number—counts the selected equal parts. Comparing amounts also requires attention to the whole: the half-versus-quarter comparison here uses pizzas of the same total size.
blocks.title: A fraction depends on the whole and an equal partition

blocks.text: Follow this sequence before naming or comparing a share. If the pieces are unequal, do not label each piece as an equal fraction merely by counting the pieces.

nodes.label: 1 → Identify the whole
nodes.detail: Use the complete pizza as the reference amount.

nodes.label: 2 → Check equality
nodes.detail: Do all pieces contain the same amount? Two pieces qualify as halves only when their amounts are equal.

nodes.label: 5 → Check the comparison basis
nodes.detail: For the amount comparison used here, confirm that the whole pizzas are the same size.

nodes.label: 6 → Compare the shares
nodes.detail: With same-sized wholes, one half is more than one quarter, and two quarters equal one half.

blocks.title: From a complete pizza to a valid fraction comparison

blocks.text:
Alex divides one complete pizza into four equal slices and takes one.

First identify the reference whole: it is the entire pizza, not the slices left after Alex takes a share. Next check the division: all four slices contain equal amounts, so fraction notation applies. Count the four parts in the whole to obtain the denominator, 4. Count the one selected part to obtain the numerator, 1. Alex’s share is therefore 1/4, read as one quarter; three slices remain.

Now compare that share with one half of a same-sized pizza. Half of a whole contains the same amount as two of its four equal quarters. Thus 2/4 and 1/2 represent equal amounts, while Alex’s single quarter contains less pizza than one half.
blocks.title: Worked example: trace Alex’s share through the sequence

blocks.text: Each strip represents a whole pizza of the same total size. The selected portions show why a half exceeds a quarter and why two quarters match a half. This comparison depends on keeping the whole size fixed.

nodes.label: 1/4: one quarter
nodes.detail: Select one of four equal parts.

nodes.label: 2/4: two quarters
nodes.detail: Select two of four equal parts; together they contain half the whole.

nodes.label: 1/2: one half
nodes.detail: Select one of two equal parts; its amount matches two quarters of a same-sized whole.

blocks.title: Same-sized wholes make the amount comparison meaningful

blocks.text:
Imagine sharing Alex’s pizza at a picnic. Before any slices are taken, the complete pizza is one whole. To share it fairly, each piece must contain the same amount of pizza. These are equal parts. A fraction describes how many equal parts of a whole are chosen.

Fair sharing helps us picture equal parts, but simply making two pieces is not enough. A cut through the centre makes two equal pieces, called halves. A cut near the edge makes a small piece and a large piece, so those pieces are not halves.
blocks.title: Think of sharing a pizza fairly

blocks.text:
Alex cuts one whole pizza into four equal slices.

First, count every slice in the whole: there are four. Write 4 at the bottom of the fraction. This bottom number is called the denominator; it counts all the equal parts.

Next, Alex takes one slice. Write 1 at the top. This top number is called the numerator; it counts the parts chosen.

Alex’s share is 1/4, read as “one quarter.” It means one of the four equal parts. Three slices remain, but the bottom number stays 4 because the whole was divided into four equal parts.
blocks.title: Follow Alex’s share, one step at a time

blocks.text:
These strips represent pizzas of the same total size. Think of the shaded parts as the slices taken. One half contains more pizza than one quarter. Two quarters together contain the same amount as one half.

The same-sized pizzas matter: the comparison here works because each whole contains the same amount of pizza.

nodes.label: 1/2 — one half
nodes.detail: One of two equal parts is selected.

nodes.label: 1/4 — one quarter
nodes.detail: One of four equal parts is selected.

nodes.label: 2/4 — two quarters
nodes.detail: Two of four equal parts are selected, making the same amount as one half.

blocks.title: Compare amounts, not just slice counts

blocks.text:
Choose a description: Sam cuts one pizza into three pieces of equal size and takes one piece. Which description is correct?
• Sam takes 1/3 because the whole has three equal parts.
• Sam takes 1/2 because two pieces remain on the plate.
• Sam takes 3/1 because the pizza has three pieces.

Now apply the idea at a new picnic. Jo and Lee have same-sized whole pizzas. Jo cuts one through its centre into two equal pieces. Lee cuts the other near its edge, making one small piece and one large piece. Identify each person’s whole and explain whose pieces are halves. Jo then takes one half, while Pat takes one of four equal slices from another same-sized pizza. Write Pat’s fraction and say who takes more pizza.

Finally, explain in your own words why two pieces are not always two halves. Use 1/4 to explain what the top and bottom numbers count, and explain why the size of the whole pizza matters when comparing shares.
